translations.text: Chapter Nine. “Why do you sit as a Christian with those who sent me to you, yet judge God’s servants like a pagan? You are not among living human beings unless you quickly burn me, a feeble old man, and eat me roasted.” When the prefect heard this, he was moved by respect for his old age. He ordered him to be taken out of his presence and brought to the bishop. The bishop, in the madness [?] of his anger, sent him away and imprisoned him in Heraclea, a city in Thrace. He remained there for two years, without being allowed to see any of his acquaintances. Since he was given no change of clothing and was infested with countless lice, one of his disciples went out and brought him a change. After that, no further change was allowed to be given to him, even through someone else. Later he became mortally ill. He forbade, under pain of anathema, his burial by adherents of the synod, or any of them ministering or offering prayer over him. So the orthodox [?] officers of the Roman army who were there took him out and buried him with candles and abundant perfumes. They wrapped and honored his body as that of a great martyr. They complained and spoke bitterly against the persecution of people such as these. Some of the faithful in the city planned to go out and take the holy man’s body.

Then the emperor, filled with anger, sent for the patriarch of the city and assailed him harshly with severe insults, saying, “You have turned the bishops away—the very bishops who, after much hard work, had barely agreed [?] to join us. Now you have turned them away from us!” In his agitation, he ordered the senate to enter the episcopal residence and judge the events that had taken place between them. The patriarch himself was also to stand trial, and if they found him at fault, he too was to be condemned.

At that time Conon was also arrested. He was the leader of the heresy of those who dare to count natures, substances, godheads, and gods in the holy Trinity, which is equal in substance. He too was arrested and imprisoned for a time in the episcopal residence, along with the others. They demanded that he draw up a written declaration as a heretic, but he resisted this and did not do it. When the victorious emperor learned of this, he swore by the Mother of God, saying, “Even if he appeals and enters the church and receives communion without drawing up a declaration of repentance, I will not enter it or receive communion in it.” Thus, because he was a heretic and a blasphemer, when Photius, the son of Belisarius’s wife, came to the imperial city at that time, Conon was handed over to him. He took him with him to Palestine and imprisoned him in the monastery called the New Monastery. He remained there for three years. Then he was released and went to the region of Cilicia.
13. Chapter Thirteen: About Sergius and Sergius, our priests, and the beatings and imprisonments they endured.
17. Chapter Seventeen: About how, as a result of this, persecutions were stirred up everywhere.

As a result of this persecution, which had been stirred up in the imperial city and was being carried out so zealously, tyrannically, and unceasingly, a fierce persecution was now stirred up throughout all the territories of the Romans, wherever orthodox believers were found. Persecution was stirred up against them through letters from John the patriarch and the others. It rose like the waves of the sea, and like the Babylonian furnace with its great blaze. But unlike that furnace, it was not fueled with reeds, branches, and other materials. This one was fueled with anger, fury, and zeal for destruction and killing, and it blazed terribly and fiercely. With these came all their accompanying evils: the plundering of movable belongings and the seizure of property on this pretext; and, secondly, confinement in cramped prisons and harsh bonds, tortures, beatings, banishments, and the rest, in every region and city and their districts.

Then all the Magi gathered and said to Khosrow their king, “O king, live forever! We have learned that the emperor of the Romans demands, compels, and forces everyone throughout his dominion to adopt his religion and his faith. He demands that the many people throughout all his territories worship—worship according to his religion. Everyone who refuses to obey him he expels and drives out of his entire dominion. Let your own divinity likewise command that the same be done in your dominion: that all religions turn to your religion, and that everyone in your dominion practice your worship. Those who dare to oppose your command must not live.”

When King Khosrow heard these things from the Magi, he yielded to their words and accepted their advice. Immediately he too began with the Christians. First he sent and seized three bishops, along with many clergy and a large crowd of people [?]. He commanded them to renounce their faith and join him in worshiping fire, the sun, and the other objects of his worship. But they disputed with him and courageously stood against him, declaring, “We are Christians, O king [?]. We worship and honor God, the maker of heaven, earth, the seas, and everything in them. We will not abandon him, the creator of everything, and worship his creatures. Do not be mistaken, O king. You have authority over our bodies, to do whatever you wish to them. But our souls belong to him and are in his hands, and you have absolutely no authority over them.”

When the king heard these things, along with many other words befitting the bishops’ witness, he gave orders, and immediately they were flayed and died. He also committed many other evil acts against the Christians, and destroyed many monasteries and churches. He bound and imprisoned many people, and his heart became arrogant. He blasphemed against Christ, saying, “Let us see what Christ, the Christians’ God, will do to me! I do not know who or what he is.”

These bishops recounted these things, along with many others that the king of the Persians said and did at this time, before Armenia surrendered to the Romans. They said that for this same reason he ordered fire temples to be built throughout Persian Armenia.

The pride in Patriarch Eutychius’s heart led him astray in many matters. From the beginning he had belonged to the heresy of the Sabbatians. When he became bishop, he wanted to conceal his heresy and please those who had appointed him, who held the Chalcedonian position. At first he stood up and vigorously championed the doctrine of two natures, and began persecuting harshly. When he was removed from his throne and went into exile, he composed a large book setting out the divisive teaching concerning two natures.

When he was recalled and returned to his throne after John’s death, as we have also explained in the preceding account, he began sending this book to the great households of senators, to men and women, especially those who recoiled from the confession of two natures. He wrote to them, “Read and learn that the church confesses two natures in Christ after the union.” But they laughed at his foolishness and sent his book back to him.

Then, after a short time had passed, he heard about the heresy of Athanasius. This man had been made the leader and founder of the heresy of those who count essences—that is, substances and natures—in the Holy Trinity. Following the error of John the Grammarian of Alexandria, he too went astray and said that these human bodies do not rise in the resurrection of the dead, but that other bodies come into being and come to the resurrection. Because of this madness of paganism and Manichaeism, a division arose among them, and they anathematized one another in writing.

When Patriarch Eutychius learned these things, he immediately joined them, became entangled with them, and became one of them. He began composing teaching on this subject and produced and published books, until his own bishops and clergy became agitated and stood against him. Much was said between them. Thus he was checked, fell silent, and put his book away, although he did not turn away from that position.

41. Chapter forty-one: Mundhir’s arrival to meet Magnus.

47. Chapter forty-seven: Emperor Tiberius and the time of his death.

Mundhir’s four sons, especially the eldest, whose name was Nu‘man—a man more cunning and better prepared for war than Mundhir himself—gathered their forces and attacked the fortress of Magnus, who had also gone up to the emperor. Without taking people captive, killing them, or burning anything, they plundered and carried off everything: gold and silver, bronze and iron, all articles of wool or linen, grain, wine, and oil. They seized all the herds of livestock of every kind that fell into their hands, all the herds of cattle, and all the flocks of sheep and goats. The Arab forces swept through and plundered all the villages of Arabia and the surrounding parts of Syria. They gathered possessions and vast quantities of booty beyond counting, then withdrew deep into the inner desert. There they established a large camp and divided the spoils, remaining alert and ready for battle and keeping watch on every side. They continued to go out, plunder, seize things, and bring them into the desert, until the whole eastern region, as far as the sea, trembled before them. People fled into the cities and did not dare to appear before them. When the rulers of the region and the commanders of the armies sent them a message asking, ‘Why are you doing all these things in this way?’ they sent back this reply: ‘Why did the emperor carry our father away like a captive, after all the labors, victories, and acts of valor in which he labored and fought on his behalf? He has cut off our allowances, and we have nothing to live on. This is why we are compelled to do these things. It is enough that we are not killing or burning.’ Finally, they went to the city of Bostra and surrounded it, saying to its inhabitants, ‘Give us our father’s weapons and the rest of the equipment of his royal office that is deposited with you. Otherwise, we will uproot, burn, and kill everything we can, both in your city and throughout its territory.’ When the military governor, a distinguished and well-known man, heard this, he became angry, gathered his army, and marched out, despising them as mere Arabs. They drew up their forces against him and overpowered him, killing him and many of his soldiers. When the inhabitants of the city saw this, they were terrified and sent them a message: ‘Stop fighting. We will give you what belongs to you. Take it in peace.’ So they brought out their father’s equipment to them. They took it and returned to their camp in the desert, but they did not stop plundering and seizing things for a long time.

When Tiberius heard these things about Mundhir’s sons, he was greatly embittered. He sent Magnus back again to make Mundhir’s brother king of the Arabs in his place, and, if he could, to subdue and capture Mundhir’s sons, whether through deceit, persuasion and disturbances, or battle. The governors of the cities and the military commanders were also ordered to accompany him with a large force, and so he went down with a great display of power. First he appointed Mundhir’s brother king; this man died twenty days later. Finally, [?] to them, to him, while [?] deceitfully.
